sections.COMMENTS:
This Composite Source straddles the region from the cities of Ancona (to the southeast) to Pesaro (to the northwest) and is part of the Umbro-Marche Apennines outer onshore thrust. This front is the NE-verging fault system at the eastern border of the Northern Apennines chain, parallel to the Marche coast.
Historical and instrumental catalogues (Boschi et al., 2000; Gruppo di Lavoro CPTI, 2004; Pondrelli et al., 2006; Guidoboni et al., 2007) show a few key earthquakes in this region, including (from southeast to northwest) the 30 October 1930 (Mw 5.9) and 2 January 1924 (Mw 5.6) Senigallia events, and the 21 September 1897 (Mw 5.5, Adriatico Centrale) one. The area also shows a sparse intermediate (4.5 < Mw < 5.0) seismicity.
The tectonic activity in this region is dominated by NW-SE trending, SW-dipping thrust-faults that control gentle folding and surface warping (for a synthesis, see Vannoli et al., 2004 and references therein), divided by NE-SW trending transverse structures that may act as segment boundaries among seismogenic faults. Although there is some debate in the literature concerning the current tectonic regime of the area, various evidence all strongly suggest that the region is undergoing NE-SW trending compression, including earthquake focal mechanisms all along the outer onshore front (Frepoli and Amato, 1997; Pondrelli et al., 2002), while borehole breakout data (Montone et al., 2004) illustrated a NW-SE trending minimum stress axis. Among other elements, the occurrence of a tsunami that was caused by the 1930 Senigallia event (Boschi et al., 1997), together with terrace warping and drainage anomalies that seemingly match the structural pattern of the growing anticlines in the subsurface (see Vannoli et al., 2004), all strongly suggest that the growing fault system is very near to the coast â€“ or just offshore.
Four main segments of this Source have been either associated with key earthquakes of the region or recognised based on their seismogenic potential. For an in-depth analysis of seismogenesis in this region, the reader can refer to the Individual Sources in this Database.
The strike of this source was based on that of the mapped regional structures. The dip was based on geological data. The rake represents pure thrusting, based on focal solutions and geological data. The minimum and maximum depth were based on subsurface data. The slip rate was based on geological data.

evidence: Based on geological data from Maesano et al. (2013).
Original elaboration based on geological data from Panara et al. (2021).

pictures.t: Map of hypocenter distribution with depth
pictures.c: Map showing in the inner Marche region deep crustal seismicity with depth ranging between 14 and 35 km. Shallower seismicity associated with compressional events is recorded in the coastal and off-shore zones (from Chiarabba et al. [2005]).

Depth distribution of deep crustal and subcrustal earthquakes and geometry of the Adria lithosphere flexured beneath the Apennines. The lowermost profile cuts across the Marche region (from Chiarabba et al. [2005]).

pictures.t: Seismogenic sources and thermal springs in the Garfagnana Area, northern Appenines
pictures.c: Relationships between tectonics and geofluids in the inner Apennines. The thermal springs are often found along main chain-perpendicular lineaments bounding large normal faults capable of Mw 7+ earthquakes (Vannoli et al., [2021])

The Stress Map of Italy shows a NE-SW compressional tectonic regime acting in the coastal Marche region. The directions of Shmin follow the trend of the Northern Apennines fronts from the southern Marche to the Po Plain (from Montone et al. [2004], modified).

pictures.t: Profile of seismic activity in the Northern Marche
pictures.c: The profile highlights the earthquake activity of the central-northern Apennines along the Coastal Thrust Front (CTF) and the occurrence of a strip of deeper events to the southwest, possibly related to the deeper portion of the same thrust (from Burrato et al. [2004]).

pictures.t: Map and section of Sn attenuation zone in Italy
pictures.c: Map and cross-sections showing Sn attenuation zone in Italy. The cross-section perpendicular to the Northern Apennines suggests the presence of a westward dipping mantle slab in this area (from Mele et al. [1997]).

pictures.t: Map showing Moho depths along the CROP3 profile
pictures.c: Moho depths estimated along the CROP03 profile. The doubling of the Moho in the Val Tiberina and the westward deepening of the Adriatic Moho seen in the Marche region suggest the  existence of a slab of Adriatic lithosphere (from Mele and Sandvol [2003]).

pictures.t: Section across the central Marche coastline from seismic reflection data
pictures.c: Eastern portion of SW-NE cross-section Anna-Burano-Perugia-Mte. Amiata obtained by Bally et al. [1986] using seismic reflection data and well logs.

pictures.t: Detail of cross section showing the hypotesized Senigallia source
pictures.c: Senigallia Source projected onto cross-section Alessandra-Orvieto of Bally et al. [1986]. Notice the coastal anticline whose growth may be driven by sustained slip along the Senigallia blind thrust fault.

pictures.t: Relationship between recent seismicity and thrust faults
pictures.c: Recent seismicity projected on geological cross sections by Lavecchia et al. [2003]. Notice the difference in depth between the Porto San Giorgio sequence, occurring in the uppermost 10 km of the crust, and the Faenza sequence, occurring at 10-12 km and 15-20 km depth.

pictures.t: Geomorphic response to anticlinal growth along the Foglia River [Vannoli et al., 2004]
pictures.c: Geomorphic response to the growth of the coastal anticline due to the activity of a seismogenic source near Pesaro (from Vannoli et al. [2004]).

pictures.t: Seismic reflection lines across the northern Apennines
pictures.c: Seismic reflection lines on which Di Bucci and Mazzoli base their interpretation for the external area of Northern Apennines: as the horizon ascribed to the Mid.-Up. Pleist. results undeformed thrusting and related folding ceased in the E. Pleist.

pictures.t: Isoseismal map of 30 October 1930 earthquake after Molin and Mucci [1990]
pictures.c: Isoseismal map of the 1930 earthquake according to Molin and Mucci [1990]. Notice that the area of maximum damage is strongly elongated in the NW-SE direction.

pictures.t: Hypothetical location of the Senigallia earthquake source
pictures.c: Hypotetical location of the Senigallia earthquake suorce  based on a seismic reflection profile. The correlative fault is a main thrust which generates long-wavelenght folds, (From Basili et al. [2004]).

pictures.t: Regional cross-sections across the Po Plain and the northern Adriatic Sea
pictures.c: Interpreted regional seismic reflection profiles straddling the full extents of the Adriatic basin, including the Po Plain and the adjacent Northern Apennines (to the west), Southern Alps (to the north), and Dinarides (to the east) (from Fantoni and Franciosi [2009]).
